nodes.label: Dilmun — the Bronze Age Gulf entrepôt
nodes.full: Dilmun, the trading state centred on Bahrain, is the middleman for Magan's copper — the third corner of the Dilmun–Magan–Meluhha triangle, and the broker Old Babylonian merchants eventually bypass to deal with Magan directly.
nodes.src: background — see the dilmun-3000bc-1200bc folio

nodes.label: Akkad and its kings
nodes.full: Sargon's trade boast and Naram-Sin's claimed conquest and diorite booty put Magan on the horizon of the world's first empire — its copper now strategically valuable, and a target.
nodes.src: background — Old Akkadian royal inscriptions (Frayne, RIME 2).

nodes.label: Meluhha — the Harappan Indus world
nodes.full: The far end of the eastern trade: the market for Magan copper and the source of the resident Indus merchants on the coast, whose own civilisation's decline pulls Magan's economy down with it.
nodes.src: background — Possehl, 'The Indus Civilization' (2002).

nodes.label: The Hafit horizon — first oasis settlement and the cairn tombs
nodes.full: Thousands of stone beehive cairns on the ridges above Al Ain and Bat mark the moment people settled the interior oases permanently. Jemdet Nasr–style Mesopotamian pottery in the tombs shows the new communities were already trading north.
nodes.src: Danish expedition to Buraimi (1959–62); K. Frifelt, 'The Island of Umm an-Nar' vol. 1 (1991). Hafit tomb pottery parallels Jemdet Nasr / ED I Mesopotamia.

nodes.label: Umm an-Nar — towers, round tombs and peak Bronze Age society
nodes.full: Named after an island off Abu Dhabi, the Umm an-Nar culture built monumental round mud-brick towers with internal wells and finely dressed circular collective tombs across the Oman peninsula. This is Magan at its height, the copper land of the Akkadian inscriptions.
nodes.src: Frifelt, 'The Island of Umm an-Nar' vols. 1–2 (1991–95); Hili excavations (S. Cleuziou); Bat World Heritage site.

nodes.label: Mannu-dannu, lord of Magan, captured by Naram-Sin of Akkad
nodes.full: Naram-Sin of Akkad records that he 'marched against Magan and personally caught Mannu-dannu, lord of Magan'. It is the only named ruler of Bronze Age Magan — preserved by the foreign king who claimed to have defeated him.
nodes.src: Naram-Sin inscription (Frayne, RIME 2.1.4); the name is given as Manium / Mannu-dannu. Whether a real conquest or a literary boast is debated.

nodes.label: The Wadi Suq reorganisation
nodes.full: After 2000 BC the towers were abandoned, settlement dispersed, and burial shifted to long above-ground tombs. Once read as a collapse, the Wadi Suq period is now seen as a rebalancing toward herding and smaller communities as the copper trade changed.
nodes.src: S. Cleuziou & M. Tosi, 'In the Shadow of the Ancestors' (2007, rev. 2020); C. Velde on the Wadi Suq reassessment.

nodes.label: Naram-Sin's campaign against Magan
nodes.full: Naram-Sin claims to have crossed the sea, defeated a coalition of Magan cities and hauled back 'Magan stone' — diorite — for his statues. Whether a real expedition or royal propaganda, it shows Magan was worth an Akkadian king's boast.
nodes.src: Naram-Sin inscriptions (RIME 2.1.4); a diorite statue base names the stone as booty from Magan. c.2254–2218 BC.

nodes.label: The Umm an-Nar towers as competitive architecture
nodes.full: Each major oasis raised one or more massive round towers, often within sight of the next. Whether forts, granaries or elite residences, their scale and visibility read as communities asserting standing against their neighbours.
nodes.src: Interpretive debate summarised in Cleuziou & Tosi (2007/2020); the towers at Hili, Bat (Kasr al-Rojoom, Kasr al-Sleme) and Tell Abraq.

nodes.label: Standardised Umm an-Nar tomb architecture
nodes.full: From Abu Dhabi to inner Oman, Umm an-Nar tombs share the same design — a ring of fitted white stone, internal partitions, a low entrance. A norm this consistent across such a wide area implies shared ideas about who built tombs and how.
nodes.src: Frifelt (1991); the Hili Grand Tomb and Tomb N; Mowaihat tomb (Ajman).

nodes.label: The round tower as communal property
nodes.full: Each Umm an-Nar tower enclosed or adjoined a well and stores, and stood at the centre of an oasis community's land. Building and maintaining a structure on that scale, and controlling the water inside it, implies rules about who held rights in the oasis and who did the work.
nodes.src: The interpretation of the towers as loci of communal water-and-land management: Cleuziou & Tosi, 'In the Shadow of the Ancestors' (2007, rev. 2020); the Bat and Hili tower complexes.

nodes.label: Umm an-Nar collective burial
nodes.full: Umm an-Nar tombs held the disarticulated remains of hundreds of people of both sexes and all ages, added over generations and periodically rearranged. Death dissolved the individual into the ancestral collective.
nodes.src: Frifelt (1995); the Hili North Tomb A (c.600+ individuals); Tell Abraq tomb (Potts, 'A prehistoric mound in the Emirate of Umm al-Qaiwain', 2000).

nodes.label: Carved facades — oryx, camels, serpents and human figures
nodes.full: The finest Umm an-Nar tombs carry relief carvings on their outer stones: files of oryx and dromedaries, coiled snakes, and pairs of human figures. They are the earliest monumental figural art of the peninsula and clearly carried meaning about the dead.
nodes.src: Hili Grand Tomb reliefs (Al Ain Museum); Frifelt on the Umm an-Nar island carved blocks.

nodes.label: Wadi Suq tombs — the collective becomes the family
nodes.full: Wadi Suq burial moved to long, narrow above-ground tombs used by smaller groups, with more attention to the individual body and its ornaments. The scale of the ancestral community that a tomb represented had contracted.
nodes.src: C. Velde, 'Wadi Suq and Late Bronze Age in the Oman peninsula' (2003); Shimal tombs (German mission).

nodes.label: The dressed-stone tombs of Umm an-Nar
nodes.full: The best Umm an-Nar tombs are built of white limestone blocks cut and smoothed to fit without mortar, their curved outer walls sometimes carved with animals. As architecture and as sculpture they are the peninsula's Bronze Age masterworks.
nodes.src: Hili Grand Tomb (reconstructed at Hili Archaeological Park); Frifelt (1991); Mowaihat tomb (Ajman Museum).

nodes.label: Umm an-Nar painted pottery and softstone vessels
nodes.full: Umm an-Nar potters made fine black-on-red painted jars, and carvers turned out chlorite (softstone) bowls incised with dot-in-circle and architectural motifs. The softstone vessels were exported the length of the Gulf as a recognised Omani product.
nodes.src: The 'série récente' softstone (Kohl; David); Umm an-Nar fine ware type series (Méry, 'Les céramiques d'Oman', 2000).

nodes.label: Wadi Suq bronzes and gold
nodes.full: Wadi Suq metalworkers produced distinctive long-bladed bronze weapons, collared vessels and gold jewellery — beaded necklaces, pendants, earrings — placed in family tombs. The craft tradition sharpened even as monumental building stopped.
nodes.src: Qattarah tomb (Al Ain); Dibba hoard; the 'Wadi Suq' bronze weapon typology (Lombard).

nodes.label: Sourcing softstone and copper ore
nodes.full: Umm an-Nar craftsmen returned to specific ore bodies and chlorite outcrops in the Hajar mountains, bypassing poorer sources — a detailed, transmitted geological knowledge of where the good rock lay, kept without writing.
nodes.src: G. Weisgerber's Oman mining surveys; provenance studies of Umm an-Nar softstone (Kohl) and copper (lead-isotope work by Begemann, Hauptmann).

nodes.label: A world at the edge of literacy
nodes.full: Despite three millennia of trade with literate civilisations, Magan produced almost no writing of its own. Accounting, water shares and genealogy were held in memory and social practice — a deliberate oral order, not a failure to learn.
nodes.src: The near-total absence of indigenous inscriptions before the Hellenistic period is a recognised feature of south-east Arabian archaeology (Cleuziou & Tosi 2007/2020).

nodes.label: Reading the sea — Bronze Age seafaring knowledge
nodes.full: To sail loaded copper ships between Magan, Dilmun and the Indus in the summer season meant knowing the monsoon winds, the coastal landmarks and the reef hazards of two seas. This navigational knowledge, held by the Magan boat crews, made the copper trade physically possible.
nodes.src: Reconstructed from the Ur III ship terminology and the bitumen-slab boat evidence from Ras al-Jinz (Cleuziou & Tosi 2007/2020; Vosmer on Bronze Age Gulf watercraft).

nodes.label: Magan copper
nodes.full: Oman's ophiolite mountains hold rich copper ore, and Bronze Age smelters at sites like Maysar turned out ingots by the tonne. 'Copper of Magan' in the Mesopotamian texts means Omani metal — the resource that made the peninsula matter to the wider world.
nodes.src: G. Weisgerber, 'Makan and Meluhha' (1984) and the German Mining Museum Oman project; Hauptmann, 'The Earliest Periods of Copper Metallurgy in Oman' (1985).

nodes.label: Direct Magan trade with Mesopotamia
nodes.full: Gudea of Lagash records diorite and copper coming 'from Magan', and Ur III and Old Babylonian merchants increasingly dealt with Magan directly rather than through Dilmun. The peninsula sold its metal without a middleman when it could.
nodes.src: Gudea Statue B (RIME 3/1.1.7); Old Babylonian 'Magan' trade texts (Leemans 1960). The shift from Dilmun-brokered to direct Magan trade.

nodes.label: The softstone vessel industry
nodes.full: Carved chlorite bowls and lids from Omani outcrops turn up from Bahrain to the Indus. It was a manufacturing export — a low-bulk, high-value product the peninsula made and shipped in quantity for over five centuries.
nodes.src: Distribution of the 'série récente' softstone (David 1996; Kohl 1975); finds at Qal'at al-Bahrain, Susa, Indus sites.

nodes.label: Aridity and the Umm an-Nar to Wadi Suq shift
nodes.full: A dry episode around 2200 BC — felt across the Near East — coincides with the abandonment of the towers and the move to a more mobile Wadi Suq economy. Whether climate or the collapse of the copper trade drove the change is still argued.
nodes.src: The 4.2 ka event and south-east Arabia (Parker et al.); the climate-vs-trade debate in Cleuziou & Tosi (2007/2020).

nodes.label: Bronze Age copper smelting at Maysar
nodes.full: The Maysar workshops preserve the full copper chain: crushed ore, tapping furnaces, tuyères, slag heaps and ingot moulds. Omani smelters were producing metal at industrial scale a thousand years before the Iron Age.
nodes.src: Hauptmann, 'The Earliest Periods of Copper Metallurgy in Oman' (1985); Weisgerber's Maysar excavations.

nodes.label: The Umm an-Nar round tower
nodes.full: Circular structures 20–40 m across, built of mud-brick or stone on a stone footing, often enclosing a well — the Umm an-Nar tower is the peninsula's signature Bronze Age building, combining water security, storage and display in one form.
nodes.src: Hili 1 (Al Ain); Bat towers (World Heritage); Tell Abraq tower (Potts). Function debated: fort, granary, elite residence.

nodes.label: Tin bronze
nodes.full: Wadi Suq smiths alloyed copper with tin — imported, ultimately, from sources as far as Central Asia — to make the harder metal of their long-bladed weapons and collared vessels. The peninsula's metallurgy kept pace with the wider Bronze Age even as its monumental building stopped.
nodes.src: Wadi Suq bronze compositional studies (Lombard); the tin-sourcing problem for Gulf Bronze Age metallurgy (Weeks, 'Early Metallurgy of the Persian Gulf', 2003).

nodes.label: Magan in the Gulf trade triangle
nodes.full: To Mesopotamia and Dilmun, Magan sent copper and diorite; back came grain, textiles, oil and finished goods. The peninsula was the third corner of the Dilmun–Magan–Meluhha network and, for copper, its most important supplier.
nodes.src: Akkadian and Ur III references to Magan; the network reconstructed in Potts, 'The Arabian Gulf in Antiquity' vol. 1 (1990).

nodes.label: Indus material and people on the Magan coast
nodes.full: Harappan black-slipped storage jars, Indus weights, a comb, ivory and Indus-style pottery made locally in Omani clay point to Indus merchants — perhaps a resident community — living on the Magan coast and handling the copper trade east.
nodes.src: Indus finds at Tell Abraq and Umm an-Nar (Potts; Méry); locally-made Indus-type 'black-slipped jars'; Ras al-Jinz bitumen and Indus links (Cleuziou & Tosi).

nodes.label: Diorite for the statues of Gudea
nodes.full: The hard black stone of Gudea of Lagash's famous seated statues was shipped from Magan. A ruler of a Mesopotamian city-state reached across the Gulf for the specific rock that would carry his image into eternity.
nodes.src: Gudea Statue B inscription names the stone from Magan; petrographic work links it to Omani gabbro/diorite sources.

nodes.label: The Akkadian Empire reaches for Magan
nodes.full: Sargon's trade boast and Naram-Sin's claimed conquest put Magan on the horizon of the world's first empire. For the peninsula it meant its copper had become strategically valuable — and a target.
nodes.src: Old Akkadian royal inscriptions (RIME 2); Naram-Sin's Magan campaign and the 'Magan stone' booty.

nodes.label: The 4.2-kiloyear drought
nodes.full: A sharp, multi-century dry phase around 2200 BC is linked to the fall of the Akkadian Empire and disruptions from Egypt to the Indus. In the Oman peninsula it brackets the end of the Umm an-Nar tower society.
nodes.src: Weiss et al. on the 4.2 ka event; south-east Arabian records in Parker & Goudie; the coincidence with the Umm an-Nar–Wadi Suq transition.

nodes.label: The Indus decline closes the eastern trade
nodes.full: As the Harappan cities unravelled, the Indus end of Magan's trade fell away. The peninsula's Wadi Suq reorientation toward herding and smaller settlements followed the loss of its biggest export markets.
nodes.src: Indus chronology (Possehl 2002); the coincident restructuring of Gulf trade (Potts 1990).

nodes.label: Everyone in the same tomb
nodes.full: Umm an-Nar burial made almost no distinction of rank, sex or age: the whole community went into a handful of great round tombs and was mingled together over generations. Identity was collective and ancestral, not individual.
nodes.src: Frifelt (1995); bioarchaeology of the Hili and Tell Abraq tomb populations (Blau; Osterholtz).

nodes.label: The cared-for woman of Tell Abraq
nodes.full: Among the Tell Abraq tomb dead is an adult woman whose skeleton shows she was paralysed from the waist down for years — probably by polio — yet survived well into adulthood. Her survival is direct evidence that this community sustained its most dependent members.
nodes.src: K. Baustian, A. Osterholtz, D. Martin, 'A Bioarchaeology of Care' analysis of the Tell Abraq individual; Osterholtz (ed.), 'Theoretical Approaches to Analysis and Interpretation of Commingled Human Remains' (2016).

nodes.label: The Wadi Suq turn to the individual body
nodes.full: Wadi Suq tombs held fewer people and gave more care to laying out the body with its own weapons and ornaments. How a person was remembered after death had shifted from 'one of the ancestors' toward 'this man, with these things'.
nodes.src: Velde (2003) on Wadi Suq mortuary practice; the reduction in tomb population size and increased individuation of grave goods.
